title: Server-side fetch destination control across resolution and redirects

threat_model.actor: Any caller able to influence a URL, host, or stored callback target that the server later fetches
threat_model.asset: Internal network reachability and the authority the server holds by network position, including instance metadata and unauthenticated internal services
threat_model.trust_boundary: The validated URL to the destination the socket actually connects to
threat_model.failure_mode: Validation is applied to a parsed URL or a resolved address that is not the one used for the request, and is not repeated for each redirect hop
threat_model.impact: The server can be induced to issue requests to internal destinations and to return or act on the response, exposing internal services and credential-bearing endpoints

required_evidence: The server issues an outbound request to a destination derived from caller-supplied data
The destination is not restricted to a fixed set of hosts fixed at deployment time

signals: A validated URL is handed to a client with redirect following enabled
Validation resolves the hostname separately from the connection, leaving a resolution gap
Only a denylist of literal hosts or prefixes is applied, without address-family and range checks
A user-registered callback URL is validated at registration and fetched later without revalidation
Delivery retries reuse a stored URL that no current check has examined
A parser or renderer resolves subresources, external entities, or remote stylesheets on its own
A headless browser or converter navigates to caller-influenced URLs outside the validated fetch helper
A preview helper validates the parsed hostname and then calls the client with redirects enabled
A preview helper passes a caller-supplied URL straight into a URL opener

boundary.subject: the fetching component and the network position it occupies
boundary.object: the destination finally connected to, after parsing, resolution, and redirects
boundary.invariant: Every connection the fetch makes, including each redirect hop, terminates at an address that passed the destination policy immediately before that connection

examples: Remote JWKS or metadata document retrieval
Retry against a stored delivery target
Avatar or attachment fetch by URL

signals: Trace the URL from the entrypoint to the client call and note every place it is re-parsed, joined, or rewritten
Record whether redirect following is enabled and whether each redirect target is revalidated before the next connection
Find fetches that bypass the validated helper entirely, including SDK clients, template renderers, and document parsers
State the destination policy as an allowlist over resolved addresses and compare it with what the code actually asserts
Look for the resolution gap where validation resolves the name once and the connection resolves it again
Decide whether status, body, timing, or error differences reach the caller, since that separates reflected from blind reachability
Identify stored callback or import URLs that were validated once at registration and are fetched repeatedly afterwards
Establish the workload's egress policy and whether link-local or internal ranges are routable from it
Point the fetch at a locally controlled server that redirects to a loopback address and record whether the second hop is attempted
Replay normalization cases — userinfo, alternate encodings, non-HTTP schemes, IPv6 and IPv4-mapped forms — through the validator alone
Within an authorized staging environment holding no production data, record only whether an internal destination is reachable, and stop there

steps: Confirm explicit authorization and aim every probe at a local server under your control, never at third-party or internal production hosts
Fetch an allowed local destination first, so a later denial can be distinguished from a broken harness
Serve a redirect from the allowed destination to a loopback or link-local address and record whether a second connection is attempted
Replay URL normalization variants through the validation function alone and record which inputs it accepts
Record the validation point, the client's redirect configuration, and whether response content reaches the caller

false_positive_filters: The destination set is a fixed allowlist known at deploy time and no caller input can introduce a new host
An egress proxy enforces the destination policy at connection time, evidenced in configuration rather than assumed from architecture diagrams
Redirect following is disabled and each hop is revalidated within the reviewed code
The workload has no route to internal ranges and the network policy is evidenced rather than inferred from the environment's name
The URL is server-derived from a trusted record and no caller-controlled path reaches the fetch
No status, body, timing, or error difference is observable to the caller, which reduces the claim to blind reachability and requires a separate impact argument

required_evidence: The caller-controlled portion of the destination and the reachable path from the entrypoint to the client call
The validation point and the connection point side by side, showing the gap between them: a redirect, a re-resolution, or a re-parse
A safe reproduction against a locally controlled destination that demonstrates the unvalidated hop
What the caller learns from the fetch and which internal destination is reachable from the workload's network position
refutation_tests: Re-read the client configuration for disabled redirects, a hop limit, or a proxy that applies the policy at connect time
Establish whether the deployment can route to the claimed internal destination at all before asserting impact
Exercise the validator in isolation on the same inputs to separate a parser weakness from a request-time weakness
Check whether an equivalent unvalidated fetch already exists on a path the reviewer assumed safe, which would move the root cause rather than remove the finding

root_causes: Validation runs against a parsed URL while the request is issued from the original string, so parser differentials decide the destination
The name is resolved once for validation and again for the connection, so the address can change between them
Redirect handling is delegated to the client, which applies no destination policy
A denylist of literal addresses stands in for an allowlist over resolved destinations
A callback URL is validated at registration and trusted indefinitely afterwards
A second fetch path — parser, renderer, or SDK — never passes through the validated helper

variant_strategy.result_contract: EXACT | VARIANT | REFUTED | BLOCKED; exact and variant matches remain hypotheses until verified

remediation.canonical_invariant: Resolve the destination, apply the policy to the resolved address, connect to that address, and repeat the whole sequence for every redirect hop
patterns: Disable automatic redirects and revalidate each hop explicitly inside a bounded loop
Pin the connection to the address that was validated so resolution cannot change between check and connect
Prefer an allowlist of destinations over a denylist of internal ranges, and reject non-HTTP schemes at the boundary
Route every outbound fetch through one egress proxy or fetch service that enforces the policy at connection time, and remove direct client use
Revalidate stored callback URLs at delivery time and on every retry, not only at registration
Remove ambient authority from the fetching workload's network position, including metadata endpoint access, so reachability alone yields little
Disable subresource and external-entity resolution in parsers and renderers, and bound what the response exposes to the caller

assertions: The vulnerable link-preview variant validates the initial host and then follows a redirect to a private address without revalidating it
The remediated link-preview variant disables redirect following and revalidates every hop within a bounded loop
The vulnerable preview variant passes a caller-supplied URL to the fetch with no scheme or destination policy
The remediated preview variant enforces an https allowlist and delegates to a fetcher that blocks private networks
Remediated variants still fetch the allowed destination, so the assertion distinguishes enforcement from an unconditional refusal

calibration.notes: This pack has not completed a reproducible benchmark run and makes no precision or recall claim.

limitations: Local reproductions show code behaviour, not whether an internal destination exists or answers in the deployed environment
Egress proxies and network policies are frequently the real control and live outside the reviewed repository
Resolution behaviour depends on the resolver, client library, and platform, so fixture results may not transfer between runtimes
Blind reachability without an observable response needs its own impact argument and must not be reported as data exposure
